To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) aspen, the most common deciduous hardwood tree in western North America, will burn only when leaf-less and the understory is dry, (2) the Rocky Mountains have a very low incidence of lightning, and (3) aspen burned frequently before Euro-American settlement, as evidenced by the fact that all fire history studies show that aspen has a fire return interval (FRI) of 3 to 10 years in the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada, and

(a) aspen and other deciduous hardwoods once burned frequently in the Rocky Mountains and the eastern U.S.; (b) the only time that aspen and other hardwoods will readily burn is in the spring before they leaf out, or in the fall after they have leafed out and the understory is killed by frost; and (c) during both those periods there are few lightning storms.
